title: Pupin loading revived: magnetic-clad interposer wires meet Heaviside condition
idea: Time travel, 1955: a telephone engineer never equalizes a lossy line, he loads it. Sputter a laminated soft-magnetic film (CoZrTa or NiFe, mu_r ~500) around long interposer/bridge wires so per-length inductance rises until R/L = G/C (the Heaviside distortionless condition), turning RC-diffusive 10-40 mm die-to-die wires into dispersion-free lines that need no CTLE/DFE and tolerate lower swing.
why: Data-movement energy and reach (fact 5): claimed 30-50% lower pJ/bit on 2.5D links and 2-3x passive reach, so more memory stacks can sit around one accelerator instead of being capped by the beachfront ring.

title: Goto's 1954 parametron reborn as phase-latched chiplet link receivers
idea: Time travel, 1955: Japanese parametron computers stored bits as the 0/pi phase of a pumped subharmonic oscillator. Send each bit as a phase and make every receiver a tiny degenerate parametric LC tank with a thin-film HZO or BST varactor pumped at 2f from one package-wide pump, so the tank amplifies and latches the incoming phase using pump energy instead of per-lane bias current.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5): parametric gain is nearly noiseless, allowing ~20-30 mV line swings; claimed 3-5x lower receiver-plus-line energy on short chiplet links, and the shared pump doubles as the clock reference.

title: Bubble-memory field drive: lid coil shifts domain-wall data conveyors
idea: Time travel, 1970s-without-DRAM: magnetic bubble memory would have won, and it moved data with a global rotating field rather than drivers. Replace each memory die's global I/O lines with perpendicular-magnetized nanowire tracks; a planar coil in the package lid supplies the pulsed field that advances every domain wall on every die one step per cycle, with MTJ readers only where tracks land on TSVs.
why: On-die/in-stack data movement and periphery (facts 5, 7, 8): no wire capacitance is charged per bit and the coil energy is amortized over ~10^8 walls moving in lockstep; claimed ~3x lower internal transfer energy and a smaller global-I/O periphery.

title: Teleprinter current loop threaded in series through every stacked die
idea: Time travel, 1955: teleprinters shared one 20 mA loop wired in series through every station. Replace the multi-drop data TSV (which every die loads in parallel) with a constant-current loop that runs down one TSV chain and back up another through all 16 dies; the talking die diverts loop current through a local shunt for one bit time and every listener senses the voltage change across its own short series segment.
why: HBM TSV tax and I/O energy (facts 5, 6): one current serves all listeners, so energy per bit stays nearly flat as stacks grow from 8 to 24 high instead of scaling with N parallel TSV loads; claimed 2-4x lower in-stack bus energy at 16-high.

title: Analog-computer lanes: each wire carries one activation as voltage
idea: Time travel, 1955: an analog-computer engineer ships a number as a voltage, not as bits. For error-tolerant AI tensors (activations, KV values) each die-to-die lane settles to one of ~64 companded levels encoding a 6-bit mantissa, read by a per-lane SAR ADC; signs and exponents stay on ordinary digital lanes, and models are fine-tuned with the measured link noise injected.
why: Data movement and bump/TSV count (facts 5, 6): ~3-6x more information per wire per transfer, so the same bandwidth needs a third of the lanes or TSVs; net energy gain hinges on ~0.5 pJ per 6-bit conversion.

title: Grid logic for stacks: AC power through few TSVs, transformers per die
idea: Time travel, 1955: utilities chose AC because transformers make high-voltage distribution cheap. Feed a memory stack with ~5 V, 50-100 MHz AC on a few TSV pairs; each die carries a thin-film air-core transformer plus synchronous rectifier that produces VDD locally, and the AC fundamental doubles as a shared frequency reference for every die, as 1950s synchronous clocks locked to the 60 Hz grid.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): ~4x less current means ~3-4x fewer power/ground TSVs and microbumps, freeing area for data lanes or a smaller base die, and a separate clock-distribution network is removed.

title: Magnonic interposer: YIG spin-wave buses move bits without charge current
idea: Time travel, 2100: a 2100 engineer moves information as spin waves, not charge. Bond a thin yttrium-iron-garnet film onto the interposer as a network of spin-wave waveguides; magnetoelectric transducers at each die launch phase-encoded spin waves and receivers detect them by interference, so long global lanes never charge a wire.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5): no CV^2 on mm-scale wires and YIG's ultra-low damping permits mm propagation; speculative claim ~10x lower energy for low-rate global control, synchronization and status traffic, with crosstalk-free crossings.

title: Epsilon-near-zero interposer plane delivers clock in phase everywhere
idea: Time travel, 2100: a metamaterials engineer distributes clock without a tree. Tune the interposer's power-ground parallel-plate cavity (via fences plus dielectric loading) to its epsilon-near-zero point at the clock frequency, where the guided wavelength becomes effectively infinite and the whole plane oscillates in phase; every die taps clock directly from the plane.
why: Interface power and wake latency: removes per-channel DLL/PLL deskew, clock-forwarding lanes and retraining (~10-20% of memory PHY power plus pins); claimed 10-15% lower link power and faster exit from power-down.

title: Superballistic vias: viscous electron flow through graphene constrictions
idea: Time travel, 2100: a 2100 engineer exploits electron hydrodynamics. In clean hBN-encapsulated graphene, electrons scatter off each other more than off the lattice and flow like a viscous fluid that passes narrow constrictions with less resistance than the ballistic limit; build micron-pitch vertical die-to-die links as stacked graphene constriction arrays operated in that regime.
why: TSV/microbump resistance at fine pitch (fact 6): copper's surface and grain scattering grows as pitch shrinks below ~2 um; speculative claim of 2-5x lower link resistance, so dense links can be driven at lower swing.

title: Elastic cloak rings make TSVs invisible to neighboring transistors
idea: Time travel, 2100: transformation elastodynamics is routine engineering by 2100. Surround each copper TSV with 2-3 concentric etched rings filled with graded-stiffness materials (porous oxide, SiCN, polymer) designed as an elastic cloak, so the Cu/Si thermal-mismatch stress field is routed around the ring and cancelled outside it.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): 5-10 um keep-out zones around each TSV waste array and periphery area; a cloak could shrink keep-out to ~1-2 um, cutting TSV area overhead 3-5x or allowing 2x TSV density for bandwidth.

title: Negative-capacitance taps subtract wire capacitance from long buses
idea: Time travel, 2100: a 2100 engineer subtracts capacitance instead of shrinking it. At intervals along long interposer and global die buses, hang stabilized negative-capacitance cells (doped-HfO2 ferroelectric in series with a small linear capacitor, biased on its negative-slope branch) between wire and ground, so their negative incremental capacitance cancels part of the wire's positive capacitance during transitions.
why: CV^2 data-movement energy (facts 5, 10): cancelling 30-50% of line capacitance cuts switching energy and delay by the same fraction without changing voltage or geometry.

title: Thermoelectric strips harvest accelerator waste heat to power memory I/O
idea: Time travel, 2100: a 2100 engineer sees a 1 kW accelerator as a small power plant. Insert thin-film thermoelectric generator strips in the heat path between the GPU's hot edge and the cold plate beside the memory stacks; the few watts they produce at ~0.3-0.5 V feed the memory PHYs' low-voltage I/O rail directly through a local low-dropout switch, with no boost conversion.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5): recovers an estimated 20-50% of HBM I/O power (several W per accelerator) from heat already being thrown away; the cost is a few kelvin of added thermal resistance that must be budgeted.

title: Single-crystal copper foil for fine bridge wiring and power RDL
idea: Time travel, 2100: to a 2100 metallurgist, polycrystalline wiring looks like cast iron. Laminate single-crystal Cu(111) foil, made by contact-free abnormal-grain-growth annealing of cheap commodity foil, onto silicon bridges and interposers and pattern sub-micron to few-micron RDL from it, so no grain boundaries scatter electrons or seed electromigration voids.
why: Interposer wire resistance and power-RDL current limits (facts 5, 6): claimed 10-25% lower resistance in sub-um bridge lines and ~10x electromigration lifetime, allowing higher current density in power RDL and therefore fewer power bumps.

title: Electrocaloric interlayers pump heat outward from the hottest stacked dies
idea: Time travel, 2100: a 2100 engineer pumps heat with electric fields. Interleave thin electrocaloric films (relaxor P(VDF-TrFE-CFE) or lead scandium tantalate) between the dies of a tall memory stack and drive them in a phased field-on/field-off cascade, so each layer rejects heat toward the cold plate and absorbs it from the die below, moving heat out of the stack interior with no fluid.
why: Thermal ceiling on stack height (facts 3, 6): claimed 10-20 K cooler inner dies, enabling 16-to-24-high stacks (more capacity per HBM site) and lower refresh rates on the hottest die.

title: Room-temperature excitonic lanes carry charge-neutral bits across interposers
idea: Time travel, 2100: a 2100 engineer sends bits as excitons. Transfer a MoSe2/WSe2 heterobilayer onto the interposer; at the transmitter an electrical pulse creates interlayer excitons (bound electron-hole pairs with a built-in dipole), gate-defined potential channels drift them to the receiving die, and a split gate dissociates them back into charge.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5): the carriers are neutral, so no wire capacitance is charged along the path; speculative claim of fJ/bit global lanes with gate-steerable routing that can be reconfigured without crosstalk.

title: 1970s thermomigration drives aluminum droplets through wafers as TSVs
idea: Time travel, 1970s-without-DRAM: GE's temperature-gradient zone melting drove aluminum droplets straight through silicon wafers in minutes, leaving p+ recrystallized columns. Do the same for memory dies: pattern Al dots, apply a ~50-100 K/mm lamp gradient, and grow junction-isolated conductive silicon columns through thinned n-type dies, with no deep RIE, liner, barrier, seed or copper plating.
why: HBM TSV tax and capital (facts 4, 6): the TSV etch/fill/CMP toolset disappears, and because the via is silicon there is almost no thermal-mismatch stress or keep-out zone; columns of a few ohms suit signal/control TSVs while copper is kept for power. Claimed ~50% lower TSV-module cost.

title: Mott-switch receivers fire on millivolt crossings of a sharp threshold
idea: Time travel, 2100: a 2100 engineer uses phase-transition devices as receivers. Each memory lane terminates in a two-terminal NbO2 or VO2 threshold switch biased just below its insulator-metal transition; its abrupt (<10 mV-wide) switching latches a full logic level when the small incoming swing pushes it over, and the clock resets it each cycle.
why: I/O energy and voltage floor (facts 5, 10): a steep, gain-free threshold allows ~50 mV line swings with no preamplifier, potentially cutting link energy ~3x.

title: Vacuum micro-channels carry field-emitted electron bunches between chiplets
idea: Time travel, 1955 meets 2100: a tube engineer would let electrons fly instead of charging wires. Etch sealed vacuum micro-channels into the interposer between dies; at the transmitter a gated nanotip field emitter launches a bunch of ~10^3 electrons per '1', which crosses 1-10 mm ballistically to a collector at the receiving die.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5): ~10^3 electrons x ~10 V is about 2 fJ/bit versus ~100-200 fJ to charge a 10 mm wire, with no RC delay; emitter lifetime and channel vacuum are the risks.

title: Flywheel logic: micro-supercapacitor under each stack carries burst current
idea: Time travel, 1955: engineers sized generators for the average load and used flywheels and accumulators for peaks. Laminate a thin-film solid-state micro-supercapacitor (MnO2 or graphene/ion-gel, ~mF/cm^2) between each memory stack and the substrate, so the package power network delivers only average current while the local capacitor supplies refresh and burst-activation peaks.
why: Bump/TSV budget (facts 6, 7): power bumps sized for peak current can shrink ~30-40%, and the freed bumps can carry data; it also trims droop-driven timing guardbands.

title: Tube top-cap power: lid feeds stack from above, bottom bumps signal
idea: Time travel, 1955: high-voltage tubes took their plate supply through a top cap, away from the signal pins in the base. Give the top die of a memory stack backside power pads and make the package lid a split copper VDD/VSS plane pressed onto them, so supply current enters from the top and descends through dedicated power TSVs while every bottom microbump is free for signals.
why: HBM TSV tax and beachfront (fact 6): a large share of base microbumps carry power; moving power to the top could add ~1.5x signal bumps per stack or allow a smaller base die, and the lid is already the thermal path.

title: Chiral edge-state lanes: one-way, reflection-free interposer wiring
idea: Time travel, 2100: a 2100 engineer wires packages with topological conductors. Pattern interposer lanes from a room-temperature quantum-anomalous-Hall material (a 2100 magnetic topological insulator) in which current flows only along one-way chiral edge channels that cannot backscatter, so lanes have no reflections, need no termination and have essentially no resistive loss along their length.
why: Interface energy (fact 5): termination and equalization power vanish and a lane's energy is set only by contact resistance; speculative, but would cut 2.5D link energy by more than 5x.

title: Reel-to-reel TAB tape replaces silicon interposer for flat memory modules
idea: Time travel, 1970s: tape-automated bonding gang-bonded calculator chips on reels. A 10-person shop runs a reel-to-reel semi-additive line (sputtered seed, laser-direct-imaged resist, Cu plating) making 20-25 um-pitch copper-on-polyimide tape, then gang-thermocompression-bonds its inner leads to a logic die and 4-8 bare LPDDR dies laid flat side by side, with no folding, no silicon and no TSVs.
why: Interposer capital and CoWoS scarcity (facts 4, 6): flex costs ~1/10 of silicon interposer per mm^2 and gives LPDDR-class memory 2-4x the per-edge bandwidth of a PCB at ~2-4 pJ/bit.

title: Micro-coax bond wires: shielded loops allow dense wire-bonded memory stacks
idea: Time travel, 1955: a 1955 engineer shields every signal with coax. After bonding a stack of LPDDR dies with ordinary 15 um wires, conformally coat them with parylene, laser-open the ground pads and sputter or electroless-plate a grounded metal shell, turning each loop into a ~50 ohm micro-coax; a small team needs only a wire bonder, a parylene coater and a sputter tool.
why: TSV tax (fact 6): shielded wires can be bonded at ~30 um pitch in 3-4 tiers and run 2-3x faster without crosstalk, giving HBM-like width from TSV-free stacks at roughly 1/10 of TSV-stack cost.

title: Anodize-patterned aluminum interposer: wires and dielectric from one film
idea: Time travel, 1955: an anodizing shop's trick for a 10-person line. Sputter 5-10 um of aluminum on a carrier, mask the conductor pattern with resist, and anodize the exposed aluminum fully into dense Al2O3, so wires and insulator come from one planar film with no etch, CMP or plating; repeat for 2-4 layers, leaving masked pillars as vias (planar routing, not a porous-alumina z-axis film).
why: Capital and scarce-resource intensity (fact 4): only sputter, wet electrochemistry and contact lithography are needed to make 5-10 um L/S chiplet-memory interposers at under 1/5 of silicon-interposer cost, using only aluminum and its oxide.

title: Plugboard interposer: generic mesh customized by laser-cut and laser-welded links
idea: Time travel, 1955: IBM tabulators were reprogrammed by rewiring plugboards. Mass-produce one generic interposer, a dense mesh of routing segments with laser-cuttable fuses and laser-weldable vertical links at every crossing; a 10-person shop customizes it for each memory-logic pairing in hours with a pulsed laser, so new designs need no new masks.
why: Capital/NRE (fact 4): mask sets and interposer NRE dominate small-run memory modules; one mask set is amortized across all customers and turnaround drops from months to days, cutting per-design cost 10-50x at a modest wire-length penalty.

title: Card-sorter controller radix-bins requests by row before issuing
idea: Time travel, 1955: Hollerith card sorters radix-sorted a deck before tabulating it. A 10-person team ships memory-controller IP (FPGA or small ASIC) that holds a deep 4-16k-entry window of latency-tolerant traffic (KV cache, embeddings, graph), radix-bins it by bank then row in one pass, and opens each row exactly once per sweep while latency-critical requests bypass.
why: Destructive read/overfetch and row hammer (facts 8, 9): claimed row-hit rate rises from ~30% to 80-95% on irregular streams, cutting activation energy ~3x, adding 20-30% effective bandwidth and greatly reducing activations per row.

title: Shrink-fit ring pre-compresses memory stacks like a gun barrel
idea: Time travel, 1955: built-up gun barrels and pre-stressed concrete keep brittle parts in compression. A small team heats an Invar/Kovar ring, slides it over a molded die stack and lets it shrink on, so every microbump joint and die interface sits in permanent compression and thermal cycling never puts them in tension.
why: Stack yield and reliability (fact 6): bump cracking and delamination are leading HBM-class failure modes; claimed 2-5x thermal-cycle life, letting small shops use thinner dies and smaller bumps with just a ring press and an oven.

title: Nanoporous gold bumps cold-weld dies at room temperature
idea: Time travel, 1955: Bell Labs knew clean gold cold-welds to itself. A 10-person team dealloys Au-Ag stud bumps in nitric acid into nanoporous gold sponges whose huge clean surface area and low yield strength cold-weld to gold pads at room temperature and ~50-100 MPa inside a nitrogen glovebox, with no solder, no CMP and no hybrid-bonding tool.
why: Capital and thermal budget (fact 4): 10-20 um-pitch die-to-die bonds made with a benchtop press, no reflow warpage on thin dies, and well under a milligram of gold per die.

title: Varactor-loaded board traces self-sharpen memory edges into solitons
idea: Time travel, 1955: varactor diodes plus Landauer-style shock-wave lines. Load long LPDDR/DDR board or substrate traces every few mm with tiny back-to-back varactor pairs (0201 parts or embedded die) whose symmetric C(V) forms a nonlinear transmission line, so both rising and falling edges self-sharpen and cancel the trace's dispersion; a small board team builds it with standard pick-and-place.
why: Data-movement reach (fact 5): claimed 1.5-2x passive reach or ~30% higher data rate on existing PCBs without DFE power, so more memory packages fit around each SoC.

title: Kinematic ball-and-pit fixtures align dies without vision bonders
idea: Time travel, 1955: instrument makers located parts by kinematic contact, not by measurement. A 10-person team KOH-etches matching pyramidal pits in alignment zones on both dies, drops in 150-300 um sapphire spheres, and lets the top die settle under light load into a deterministic ~0.3-0.5 um registration before a simple press bond.
why: Capital intensity (fact 4): replaces $1-3M high-accuracy bonders with etched features and fixtures, putting 10-20 um-pitch die-to-die memory interfaces within reach of a small shop.

title: Vacuum-pressure impregnation underfills dozens of stacks at once, void-free
idea: Time travel, 1955: transformer winders vacuum-pressure-impregnate coils so varnish reaches every gap. A 10-person team loads a batch of bonded memory stacks into a chamber, evacuates it, floods it with low-viscosity (<50 mPa s) filled resin, then pressurizes to 5-10 bar to drive the resin into 5-10 um inter-die gaps before curing.
why: Stack yield (fact 6): voids under fine-pitch bumps cause bridging and cracks; batch VPI replaces slow capillary underfill and MUF lines, claiming +5-10 points of stack yield with a ~$100k chamber.

title: Cleaved synthetic mica sheets as flat, cheap interposer substrates
idea: Time travel, 1955: silver-mica capacitor makers split mica into micron-thin films. A 10-person shop cleaves US-made synthetic fluorophlogopite into atomically flat 15-30 um sheets, laser-drills vias and patterns thin-film copper on both faces, making a k~6, low-loss interposer whose flatness comes from cleaving rather than grinding or CMP.
why: Interposer scarcity and capital (facts 4, 6): a silicon-free, glass-free substrate for chiplet-memory modules at roughly 1/10 of the tool investment, with no Spruce Pine quartz in the chain.

title: Diamond fly-cutting planarizes bonding surfaces without CMP slurry
idea: Time travel, 1955: record-mastering lathes cut mirror-flat surfaces with a single diamond. A small team uses an ultra-precision diamond fly-cutter to plane copper pads and the surrounding polymer or oxide in one dry pass to nm-scale flatness, preparing memory and logic dies for direct Cu-Cu bonding without CMP tools, slurry or post-CMP clean.
why: Capital and consumables (fact 4): CMP lines and slurry supply are major costs of fine-pitch bonding; a single planer gives small shops a path to sub-10 um-pitch memory-logic bonds.

title: Swaged copper micro-eyelets make plating-free power vias under memory
idea: Time travel, 1955: early boards made through-connections with crimped brass eyelets. A 10-person team laser-drills a thin 100-200 um core, gang-inserts tape-fed copper micro-tubes and swages them flat, forming solid-wall through-vias at 150-250 um pitch for power delivery beneath memory stacks and modules.
why: PDN resistance and process capital: solid swaged copper beats plated barrels on resistance and current capacity and needs no plating chemistry line; claimed ~2x via current capacity, so fewer power vias and bumps are needed.

title: Zone-rate memory channels: each clocked to its own trace's limit
idea: Time travel, 1970s-without-DRAM: disks would have been main storage, and disk engineers zone-recorded outer tracks at higher density. A 10-person team builds controller firmware/IP that trains each independent LPDDR channel to the highest rate its own trace length and eye allow, instead of one worst-case clock for all, and weights scheduler traffic by channel speed.
why: Data-movement bandwidth (fact 5): recovers the 15-30% of aggregate bandwidth lost to worst-case uniform clocking on boards where channel lengths differ 2-3x, with no new silicon.

title: Calculator-style chip-on-board LPDDR glob-topped beside the accelerator die
idea: Time travel, 1970s: calculator and watch makers wire-bonded bare dies straight onto the board under an epoxy glob. A 10-person team wire-bonds bare LPDDR5X dies directly onto the accelerator's organic package substrate 5-8 mm from the SoC and glob-tops them, with no memory package and no interposer.
why: Cost and pJ/bit (facts 4, 5): removes memory-package cost (~10-20%) and shrinks traces to millimeters for ~2-4 pJ/bit versus 10-20 for DDR5 modules, giving near-HBM energy at LPDDR cost with a wire bonder and dispenser.

title: Oven-stabilized memory module holds DRAM at one fixed temperature
idea: Time travel, 1955: precision crystal oscillators lived in thermostatic ovens. A small team builds modules with a thin-film heater and PID loop that hold every DRAM package at a constant ~60 C under any load, so link training, drive strength and timing are calibrated once and the guardband reserved for temperature drift is removed.
why: Interface energy: temperature-drift guardbands consume ~10-15% of timing/voltage margin; recovering them allows lower VDDQ or higher rate (~10% I/O energy) and eliminates periodic retraining stalls.

title: Vampire-tap memory bus: stubless piercing taps on one continuous line
idea: Time travel, 1970s: Xerox's thick Ethernet attached stations by piercing a continuous coax without cutting it. A 10-person team builds memory channels as one unbroken impedance-controlled flat cable, and each module attaches through an insulation-piercing micro-tap with an integrated series resistor right at the conductor, so there are no stubs or branches and 4-8 modules share a channel at full speed.
why: Capacity per channel: stub reflections limit today's buses to 1-2 modules per channel at high speed; stubless taps could give 2-4x capacity per CPU socket from commodity DRAM without CXL hardware.

title: Repeater-in-the-cable memory: DRAM overmolded into GPU flyover cables
idea: Time travel, 1955: TAT-1 (1956) put its vacuum-tube repeaters inside the submarine cable itself. A 10-person cable-assembly shop overmolds LPDDR packages plus a small buffer/retimer controller into the backshells of the copper flyover and backplane cables between accelerators, so each cable is also a memory tier that can park in-flight data (KV spills, pipeline activations) one hop from both ends.
why: Capacity without board area or extra boxes: tens of GB per rack in volume that is empty today, and staged transfers cut repeated trips to host DRAM; uses new commodity LPDDR, not reclaimed DIMMs.

title: Metered data movement: tenants billed per byte moved and activation
idea: Time travel, 2100: by 2100, data movement is billed like electricity. A 10-person team ships a hypervisor/driver agent that reads memory-controller performance counters, meters each tenant's DRAM/HBM bytes moved and row activations, and prices them on time-of-use tariffs, so customers are paid to pick memory-frugal kernels, batch sizes and quantization.
why: Demand-side supply increase: if 10-20% of memory traffic and footprint is avoidable once it has a price, a fleet gains that much effective capacity and bandwidth without new fabs.

title: Ferrite-bead lesson: lossy film absorbs reflections, replacing termination current
idea: Time travel, 1955: TV designers slipped ferrite beads onto leads to kill ringing. A small team dispenses a thin NiZn-ferrite/polymer film over the last 1-2 mm of each memory line at the receiver pad; its permeability turns highly lossy above ~1 GHz, so reflected high-frequency energy becomes heat while the bus runs unterminated with no on-die-termination DC current.
why: I/O energy (fact 5): on-die termination is a large part of high-rate LPDDR/DDR I/O power; a passive absorber could cut I/O power ~20-30%.

title: Ultrasonic fluxless bumping wets solder straight onto aluminum pads
idea: Time travel, 1955: aluminum was soldered without flux by ultrasonic tinning irons that cavitated the oxide away. A 10-person team bumps commodity DRAM/LPDDR dies, which ship with aluminum pads, using an ultrasonic solder-jet or dip head that breaks the Al2O3 and wets Sn-Zn solder directly onto the pad, with no sputtered UBM, no plating line and no flux residue to clean.
why: Capital and access (fact 4): bumping gatekeeps flip-chipping of purchased dies; removing UBM and plating lets small teams flip-chip commodity memory beside logic at short reach (~2-4 pJ/bit).
